common_name: ColorBlaze El Brighto Coleus (Tricolor Purple-Red and Gold Sun-Tolerant Coleus)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; El Brighto's tricolor variegation intensifies with more direct sun while still performing well in partial shade.

directions: ColorBlaze El Brighto grows into an upright, well-branched plant clothed in boldly variegated leaves that combine deep purple-red centers with bright yellow-to-orange margins, a more electric look than solid-colored ColorBlaze selections. Pinch the stem tips while plants are young to build denser branching, and remove any flower spikes promptly, since the plant blooms very late and foliage is the entire point. Grow in partial shade to sun-dappled exposure in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil, where the tricolor pattern grows brighter with more light while staying resistant to scorch. It works well as a repeating accent through sunny-to-lightly-shaded borders or as a dramatic thriller in mixed containers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant

common_name: ColorBlaze Rediculous Coleus (Award-Winning Solid Deep Red Sun-and-Shade Coleus)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after all frost danger has passed; Rediculous tolerates both sun and shade equally well, making placement flexible in mixed beds and containers.

directions: ColorBlaze Rediculous forms a dense, well-branched mound of solid deep red foliage that holds its saturated color from spring through fall without fading in summer heat. It rarely sends up flower spikes, so little deadheading is needed to keep the plant's energy focused on leaf production. Because it performs equally well in full sun and shade, it is one of the more flexible ColorBlaze selections for mixed plantings, suiting both container thrillers and mass landscape color blocks. Provide rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil and pinch stem tips periodically on young plants to encourage a fuller shape.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Coleus scutellarioides cultivars

common_name: Premium Sun Lime Delight Coleus (Solid Chartreuse Seed-Grown Sun Coleus)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, pressing the fine pelleted seed onto the mix surface since light aids germination; transplant once nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Premium Sun Lime Delight forms a dense, mounded plant clothed entirely in bright, unmarked chartreuse-green leaves that glow against darker-foliaged companions. Start the fine seed indoors on the surface of a moist mix, since germination depends on light, then transplant once nights stay warm. Its breeding for full-sun tolerance lets it hold color without the scorch that limits older seed coleus strains in open beds, while it also performs well in partial shade. Pinch young plants and remove any flower spikes promptly to maintain the tidy, bushy habit through the growing season.

common_name: Supertunia Saffron Finch Petunia (Sunny Yellow Rounded Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after all frost danger has passed in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest flower coverage.

directions: Supertunia Saffron Finch bears clear, sunny yellow blooms on a full, well-branched, rounded habit that stays lower and tidier than the outsized Vista series, making it useful for front-of-border plantings and smaller container combinations. It self-cleans without deadheading and keeps producing new flowers through summer heat when watered consistently and fed on a regular schedule. Plant vegetatively propagated transplants in full sun after frost danger has passed, siting it where its warm yellow tone can play off purple or blue companion plants. Light afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps keep the color from washing out.

common_name: Supertunia Bermuda Beach Petunia (Rare Pastel Salmon-Coral Spreading Petunia)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated transplants after all frost danger has passed in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom coverage.

directions: Supertunia Bermuda Beach carries an unusual salmon-coral bloom color with a soft pastel cast that sets it apart from the brighter pinks and reds common across the Supertunia line. Its mounding, moderately trailing habit spreads less aggressively than the vigorous Vista series, which keeps it easier to scale in mixed containers and smaller beds. The free-flowering plant needs no deadheading and holds its color well through summer heat given regular watering and feeding. Grow in full sun for the best bloom coverage, and pair it with deeper-toned companions to set off its unusual pastel tone.

common_name: Beacon Blue Pearl Impatiens (Downy-Mildew-Resistant Lavender-Violet Bedding Impatiens)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on the surface of moist mix, since light aids germination; hold off transplanting until nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Beacon Blue Pearl brings a soft lavender petal tone with a pearlescent sheen and a deeper violet-rose throat to the AAS-winning Beacon series, giving growers a cooler-toned option alongside the series' reds, corals, and oranges. Like its siblings it carries strong resistance to impatiens downy mildew, the disease that devastated most seed-grown Impatiens walleriana plantings after 2011, so color holds steady through humid summer stretches. Transplant into consistently moist, fertile, well-drained soil in shade, keeping foliage dry when watering to further limit disease pressure. Its compact, mounded habit fills beds and containers quickly once nights stay warm.

common_name: Beacon Rose Impatiens (Downy-Mildew-Resistant Deep Rose-Pink Bedding Impatiens)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on the surface of moist mix, since light aids germination; hold off transplanting until nights stay reliably warm.

directions: Beacon Rose carries saturated rose-pink flowers on the same tidy, mounded plant that defines the rest of the AAS-winning Beacon series, filling out the line's warm-pink color range alongside Coral, Lipstick, and Salmon. Bred for strong resistance to impatiens downy mildew, it keeps blooming reliably through the humid, rainy stretches that once devastated seed-grown Impatiens walleriana beds. Set transplants into evenly moist, fertile, well-drained soil in shade, watering at the base to keep foliage dry. Because it establishes quickly from seed, beds and containers fill in with dense color within a few weeks of transplanting.

common_name: Profusion Yellow Zinnia (Compact Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow once nights stay reliably warm, or transplant seedlings started a few weeks earlier indoors.

directions: Profusion Yellow produces clear, true-yellow single blooms on the same wide, well-branched mound that defines the rest of the Profusion series, rounding out the line's warm color range alongside Orange, Fire, and Cherry. Direct sow shallowly in full sun once the soil has warmed, or set out seedlings started a few weeks earlier indoors. Like its series-mates it shrugs off the heat, humidity, and powdery mildew that limit older garden zinnias, blooming nonstop from early summer into fall with only light, infrequent watering. Deadheading is unnecessary since spent blooms are quickly hidden by new growth.

common_name: Profusion Lemon Zinnia (Compact Pale Yellow Disease-Resistant Single Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow once nights stay reliably warm, or transplant seedlings started a few weeks earlier indoors.

directions: Profusion Lemon offers a lighter, brighter take on yellow than the deeper-toned Profusion Yellow, with pale lemon-yellow single blooms held on the same wide, mounded, well-branched plant that defines the series. Direct sow shallowly once the soil has warmed in spring, or transplant seedlings started a few weeks earlier indoors for an earlier start. It shares the series' strong heat tolerance and resistance to the powdery mildew and leaf spot that slow down older garden zinnias, flowering heavily from early summer until frost with minimal watering once established. Its compact, uniform habit works equally well in landscape borders, mixed containers, and vegetable garden plantings for pollinators.
